title: Probability and stochastic processes
organizing_question: What is the complete law, and which operations preserve or transform the uncertainty needed by the question?
overview:
The probability material is organized by mathematical operation rather than by a single chronological narrative. A model first specifies its sample space and law. Expectations then integrate against that law, dependence connects its coordinates, transitions evolve it in time, and limit theorems approximate it under explicit scalings. This order makes the archive readable without making every probabilistic topic an instance of one favored physical metaphor. The four families progress from compatible outcomes to combinatorial randomness, from processes to asymptotic simplification.

The first family supplies the indispensable foundation. Marginal event probabilities determine an expected count but usually leave the probability of complete success unresolved. Population weights enter an expected square through square roots in its Euclidean representation; amplitude attenuation is a different operation. Posterior predictive dependence gives a second mechanism: future outcomes independent conditional on a latent parameter become dependent after it is integrated out. These exact finite distinctions continue through the three-item surplus model at the end of the source period. Their significance is constructive: the revised question can ask for the range over all admissible couplings instead of assuming an unprovided independence law.

Random sampling and filtrations move the same discipline into combinatorics and topology. Weighted fixed-cardinality samples are normalized by elementary symmetric polynomials, and inclusion probabilities yield expected Euler characteristic by linearity. A random barcode needs more: the actual birth rule and boundary ranks. The four-cycle fixture makes one complete persistence distribution accessible, while the general weighted formula remains an explicit mathematical recipe. This is an important boundary between a finite worked lab and a universal persistent-homology tool.

Stochastic dynamics specify how the law changes. A generator determines expectation evolution, while Itô's second derivative produces an extra term invisible to deterministic differentiation. The OU process provides exact solutions, stationary variances and a transparent comparison with Euler–Maruyama. Linear SDE propagation separates present posterior uncertainty from fresh process noise. Sensor choices are meaningful only when compared against one prior, one target and one terminal horizon. A driver sensor can beat a direct present-target sensor for predicting a future target without violating any monotonicity theorem.

The final family studies simplification under scaling. Finite variance yields the Gaussian averaging fixed point; Cauchy stability shows why that conclusion cannot be universal. Logarithms turn random products into sums with their own transform threshold. Trace-summable Gaussian covariances permit genuine Hilbert-space samples, whereas finite-dimensional consistency alone permits only cylindrical data. Direct couplings give a different approximation method, bounding Lipschitz observables without a central limit theorem. Across all four families, exact finite identities, limiting laws, numerical approximations and empirical calibration remain distinct claims. The atlas executes representative model checks and labels the broader extensions as recipes.
core_objects: Finite laws and couplings; moments and characteristic functions; weighted subset measures; random filtrations; Markov generators; Wiener integrals; Gaussian covariance operators.
open_frontier: Combine exact finite combinatorial expectations with quantitative approximation of stochastic dynamics, retaining explicit dependence, topology and error metrics rather than replacing them by one scalar uncertainty score.

title: Information, statistics and inference
organizing_question: What does the available observation distinguish, and what claim does its evidence actually justify?
overview:
Information and inference begin with an observation map and a target. The map decides which states can be distinguished; the target and loss decide whether those distinctions matter. A sampling law then determines which statistical guarantees are available. This domain therefore organizes covariance, entropy, diagnostics and validation around a sequence of questions: what remains hidden, what transformation loses information, what a finite sample can establish, and what a summary preserves. These questions connect closely but their answers are not interchangeable.

Covariance geometry is the first layer. A covariance is a positive semidefinite quadratic form when second moments exist. Null directions record exact linear dependence, and positive averaging preserves the covariance cone. Nonlinear maps add a decisive qualification: a vanishing Jacobian can conceal a nonzero leading uncertainty at the next order. The squared-Gaussian example is fully calculable. It then becomes a hidden-target model, where observing one coordinate perfectly still leaves a squared hidden coordinate random. Conditional expectation gives the optimal estimator and an exact orthogonal decomposition of risk. This identifies separately the part due to structural invisibility and the part due to measurement noise.

Entropy and information geometry describe how laws compare. Relative entropy contracts under a specified stochastic channel; Shannon entropy increases under doubly stochastic mixing but can decrease on approach to a concentrated equilibrium. Mutual information is statistical dependence, not a causal arrow. In parameter space, local KL expansion produces the Fisher quadratic form, with a null direction for common softmax logits. These results explain what may be monitored during optimization while preserving the need to evaluate actual prediction loss independently. Matrix entropy has related exact identities, but the quantum algebra and positivity hypotheses remain visible.

Statistical inference adds sampling and selection. Identifiability is a statement about whether parameters produce distinct observation laws at the stated design. Calibration is a statement about a test statistic under a null. Generalization is a statement about unseen draws. A nested fit automatically improves training residuals, and a prescribed spectrum can always be embedded in a matrix; neither fact proves prediction. Finite uniform bounds and PAC–Bayes methods supply genuine guarantees under declared bounded-loss sampling models. Exact paired randomization supplies another route when the sign-exchangeability null is justified. Its finite p-value remains separate from effect magnitude and practical benefit.

The final family treats the capacity and limitations of summaries. Lossless reconstruction requires an injective encoding and therefore a counting lower bound. Prefix entropy grows by conditional information, independently of a chosen symbolic metric. Spectral flatness, circular concentration, AUROC and pooled correlation each retain particular features and discard others. Their precise invariances are useful; promoting one to a universal certificate is not. The resulting interactive direction is a panel of observation fibres, conditional-risk calculations and finite diagnostic populations. The current atlas supplies small verified fixtures and cross-links to observability and exact-counting labs, while general statistical estimation and historical empirical validation remain unclaimed.
core_objects: Observation sigma-algebras; conditional expectation and Bayes risk; PSD covariance; KL divergence and channels; Fisher matrices; iid validation laws; randomization populations; finite encodings and diagnostic invariants.
open_frontier: Design observations sufficient for a specified target or action, then combine exact structural guarantees with independent finite-sample calibration without conflating identifiability, uncertainty and predictive performance.

title: Optimization and decision theory
organizing_question: Which objective, feasible set and certificate turn a proposed choice into a justified global decision?
overview:
Optimization unifies much of the archive only after its inputs are typed. An objective assigns preference, a feasible set defines admissible alternatives, and a certificate supplies a bound valid over all of them. Algorithms search for candidates but do not replace these definitions. This domain is arranged from global convex certificates through constructive updates and finite search to robust decisions under shared uncertainty. It connects the practical question of choosing an action with the mathematical question of which uncertainties can change that action.

Convex duality supplies the cleanest starting point. A feasible primal point and a feasible dual bound can prove global optimality when their values agree. The constrained covariance quadratic makes nullspaces central: a feasible zero-energy null vector changes the answer completely, while a budget orthogonal to the nullspace leads to a pseudoinverse formula. Fenchel conjugates expose the effect of domains and nonsmooth penalties. An SDP zero-gap pair provides a finite exact certificate even when an iterative solver's convergence is irrelevant. In contrast, a stationary cubic equation or an indefinite quadratic requires a separate global analysis.

Proximal and projected methods turn an objective into a reproducible update. Soft thresholding, radial shrinkage and ridge scaling differ because their regularizers differ. The projection variational inequality and smooth descent lemma give a direct finite-step bound. A resolvent step damps curvature according to its eigenvalues and needs a positive quadratic model. Graph heat flow makes the distinction between continuous dissipation and discrete stability explicit. Metric projections, subspace restrictions and Wasserstein pushforwards add useful geometry while preserving their own feasibility and contraction hypotheses. These ideas explain why clipping a gradient, projecting a state and constraining a trajectory are different operations.

Objective design and finite search then expose the combinatorial side. The total-scatter identity can collapse seemingly independent clustering weights into the same objective. Capacity constraints and weighted preferences require different formulations. Pareto nondominance contains legitimate alternatives that no positive linear selector can choose. Exact QUBO enumeration and min-plus transfer provide finite certificates of a chosen problem. Frontier and equivalence-class compression are valid when they preserve complete continuation behavior, not merely a current best answer. Search error, physical-model error and measurement error consequently remain separate parts of an implementation claim.

The final family asks for the cheapest information that settles a decision. When two scores share nuisance uncertainty, subtract them at the same state before optimizing. Their joint difference can have a strict positive lower bound even when separately computed intervals overlap widely. Measurements restrict the compatible-state set, and a finite experiment tree can stop when each remaining fibre certifies one action. The implemented L08 model makes this cancellation visible without claiming a general optimizer or empirical forecast. This endpoint joins the other domains: exact counting can enumerate alternatives, observability can expose decisive fibres, covariance can describe noise, and duality can certify a robust margin. The result is an organized program of mathematical choices whose guarantees state their actual scope.
core_objects: Convex objectives and conjugates; affine constraints and PSD cones; primal-dual gaps; proximal maps and variational inequalities; finite Pareto sets; frontier signatures; common uncertainty sets and robust margins.
open_frontier: Construct exact positivity and dual certificates for nonlinear decision differences, then optimize finite measurement trees whose outcome fibres preserve those certificates at minimum guaranteed cost.
